prompt: The Mathematical Kangaroo takes place each year on the third Thursday of March. What is the latest possible date on which the competition could take place?

solutions.title: Latest first Thursday
solutions.body:
The first Thursday of March is one of 1–7 March, so it is at the latest 7 March. The third Thursday is two weeks later: at the latest $7 + 14 = 21$ March.

**Answer: (D) 21 March**

solutions.title: Count days
solutions.body:
The third Thursday has exactly two Thursdays before it in March, so at most $2 \cdot 7 = 14$ days of March come before the week containing it, plus up to 6 more days of that week. The latest date is $14 + 7 = 21$ March (this happens when 1 March is a Friday).

**Answer: (D) 21 March**

prompt: How many quadrilaterals of any size are to be found in the diagram pictured?

solutions.title: Check pairs of lines
solutions.body:
The picture is two overlapping rectangles standing on the same bottom line: a wide one on the left and a taller, narrower one on the right. Every quadrilateral in it must be a rectangle whose four sides are drawn lines.

- Top = the top of the tall rectangle: only the tall rectangle itself fits (the vertical lines of the wide rectangle don't reach that high). **1**
- Top = the top of the wide rectangle: this line runs from the left side of the wide rectangle to its right side, crossing the left side of the tall rectangle. Choosing two of these three vertical lines as sides gives the wide rectangle, its left part and the middle overlap. **3**
- No rectangle has both tops as sides, because the top of the wide rectangle does not reach the right side of the tall one.

Total $1 + 3 = 4$.

**Answer: (D) 4**

prompt: What is the answer to $2014 \times 2014 \div 2014 - 2014$?

solutions.title: Order of operations
solutions.body:
Multiplication and division first, from left to right: $2014 \times 2014 \div 2014 = 2014$. Then $2014 - 2014 = 0$.

**Answer: (A) 0**

prompt: The area of rectangle $ABCD$ in the diagram is 10. $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AD$ and $BC$ respectively. How big is the area of the quadrilateral $MBND$?

solutions.title: Half of the rectangle
solutions.body:
$MN$ cuts the rectangle into two equal halves $ABNM$ and $MNCD$, each of area 5.

The diagonal $MB$ halves the rectangle $ABNM$, so triangle $MBN$ has area $2.5$. Likewise diagonal $ND$ halves $MNCD$, so triangle $MND$ has area $2.5$.

$MBND = 2.5 + 2.5 = 5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

solutions.title: Subtract the corners
solutions.body:
The parts of the rectangle outside $MBND$ are the triangles $ABM$ and $NCD$. Each is a right triangle with legs $AB$ and $\tfrac12 AD$, so each has area $\tfrac14$ of the rectangle, i.e. $2.5$.

$MBND = 10 - 2.5 - 2.5 = 5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

prompt: The product of two natural numbers is 36, and their sum 37. How big is the (positive) difference between the two numbers?

solutions.title: Find the numbers
solutions.body:
Pairs with product 36: $1 \cdot 36$, $2 \cdot 18$, $3 \cdot 12$, $4 \cdot 9$, $6 \cdot 6$. Only $1 + 36 = 37$. Difference $36 - 1 = 35$.

**Answer: (E) 35**

prompt: Wanda has lots of pages of square paper, whereby each page has an area of 4. She cuts each of the pages into right-angled triangles and squares (see the left hand diagram). She takes a few of these pieces and forms the shape in the right hand diagram. How big is the area of this shape?

solutions.title: Area of each piece
solutions.body:
A page has side 2. It is cut into:
- a large right triangle (half the page): area 2;
- a small square of side 1: area 1;
- two small right triangles with legs 1: area $\tfrac12$ each.

The shape on the right consists of 1 large triangle (the one along the long diagonal), 2 small squares and 4 small triangles:

$2 + 2 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot \tfrac12 = 6$.

**Answer: (E) 6**

solutions.title: Count unit squares
solutions.body:
Use the small square (area 1) as a unit. The large triangle is two unit squares' worth, each small triangle is half a unit square. In the shape: 2 unit squares $+$ 1 large triangle (2) $+$ 4 small triangles (2) $= 6$.

**Answer: (E) 6**

prompt: A bucket is filled halfway with water. A cleaning liquid fills another 2 litres of liquid into the bucket. Now the bucket is three-quarters full. How many litres of water in total can fit into the bucket?

solutions.title: Fraction of the bucket
solutions.body:
The 2 litres raised the level from $\tfrac12$ to $\tfrac34$ full, i.e. by $\tfrac14$ of the bucket. So the whole bucket holds $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ litres.

**Answer: (B) 8 Litre**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
If the bucket holds $V$ litres: $\tfrac12 V + 2 = \tfrac34 V$, so $\tfrac14 V = 2$ and $V = 8$.

**Answer: (B) 8 Litre**

prompt: George builds the sculpture shown from seven cubes each of edge length 1. How many more of these cubes must he add to the sculpture so that he builds a large cube of edge length 3?

solutions.title: Count cubes
solutions.body:
A cube of edge length 3 is made of $3^3 = 27$ unit cubes. The sculpture (a centre cube with one cube on each of its six faces) uses 7, and all 7 lie inside the $3 \times 3 \times 3$ cube. He needs $27 - 7 = 20$ more.

**Answer: (E) 20**

prompt: Which of the following sums gives the biggest answer?

solutions.title: Factor out 11 · 111
solutions.body:
Every product is $11 \cdot 111 \cdot k$:
- $44 \cdot 777 = 11 \cdot 111 \cdot (4 \cdot 7) = 11 \cdot 111 \cdot 28$
- $55 \cdot 666 = 11 \cdot 111 \cdot 30$
- $77 \cdot 444 = 11 \cdot 111 \cdot 28$
- $88 \cdot 333 = 11 \cdot 111 \cdot 24$
- $99 \cdot 222 = 11 \cdot 111 \cdot 18$

The largest is $55 \times 666$.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Gray and white pearls are threaded onto a string. Tony pulls pearls from the ends of the chain. After pulling off the fifth gray pearl he stops. At most, how many white pearls could he have pulled off?

solutions.title: Try every split
solutions.body:
Reading the string from left to right (G = gray, W = white):

G W G W W W G G W W G G G W G W G W W G

Suppose he takes $a$ gray pearls from the left end and $5 - a$ from the right end. Before he reaches the next gray pearl on a side he may also take the white pearls lying in front of it, except on the side from which the last (fifth) gray pearl comes, since he stops at once.

Whites that can be taken from the left with $a$ grays (including the whites after the $a$-th gray): $a=0$: 0, $a=1$: 1, $a=2$: 4, $a=3$: 4, $a=4$: 6.
From the right with $b$ grays: $b=0$: 0, $b=1$: 2, $b=2$: 3, $b=3$: 4, $b=4$: 4.

Best: 3 grays from the left (whites in front of the 3rd gray: 4) and 2 grays from the right, taking the whites in front of the 3rd gray from the right as well (3), finishing with the 3rd gray on the left: $4 + 3 = 7$. Checking the other splits the same way, none gives more than 7.

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt: Max has a one hour piano lesson twice a week, Hanna only has a one hour lesson every second week. The piano lessons run over a particular number of weeks. How many weeks is this, if during this time Max has 15 more hours of lessons than Hanna?

solutions.title: Difference per week
solutions.body:
Per week Max has 2 hours and Hanna $\tfrac12$ hour, a difference of $\tfrac32$ hours. To reach 15 hours: $15 \div \tfrac32 = 10$ weeks.

**Answer: (E) 10 Weeks**

solutions.title: Two-week blocks
solutions.body:
In every two weeks Max has 4 lessons and Hanna 1, so Max gets 3 more. 15 more hours needs $15 \div 3 = 5$ blocks, i.e. 10 weeks.

**Answer: (E) 10 Weeks**

prompt: Five circles each with an area of 1 cm² overlap each other to form the figure in the diagram. The sections where two circles overlap each have an area of $\frac{1}{8}$ cm². How big is the area which is completely covered by the figure in the diagram?

solutions.title: Subtract double counting
solutions.body:
The five circles stand in a row and each overlaps its neighbour, so there are 4 overlaps. Adding the five areas counts each overlap twice, so subtract each once:

$5 \cdot 1 - 4 \cdot \tfrac18 = 5 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac92$ cm².

**Answer: (B)** $\frac{9}{2}$ cm²

solutions.title: Count pieces
solutions.body:
The two end circles each have one overlap, so $1 - \tfrac18 = \tfrac78$ of each is covered only once. The three middle circles have two overlaps each: $1 - \tfrac28 = \tfrac68$ covered once. The 4 overlaps add $\tfrac18$ each.

$2 \cdot \tfrac78 + 3 \cdot \tfrac68 + 4 \cdot \tfrac18 = \tfrac{14 + 18 + 4}{8} = \tfrac{36}{8} = \tfrac92$ cm².

**Answer: (B)** $\frac{9}{2}$ cm²

prompt: A grandmother, her daughter and her granddaughter find that the sum of their ages is 100. Also each age is a power of two (that is, several two's multiplied together). How old is the granddaughter?

solutions.title: Binary
solutions.body:
The powers of two are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. The three women belong to different generations, so their ages are different powers of two. Writing 100 as a sum of different powers of two is the binary expansion $100 = 64 + 32 + 4$, and it is unique.

So the ages are 64, 32 and 4: the granddaughter is 4.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: 5 congruent rectangles are positioned in a square with side length 24 as shown in the diagram. How big is the area of one of these rectangles?

solutions.title: Two equations
solutions.body:
Let each rectangle be $a$ long and $b$ wide. The rectangles form a staircase from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner.

Going across the square from left to right along the staircase we pass, in order, the gap to the left of the lower upright rectangle (width $b$, the same as the upright rectangle's width), the middle lying rectangle ($a$), the upper upright rectangle ($b$) and the top lying rectangle ($a$): $2a + 2b = 24$.

The bottom lying rectangle exactly spans that left gap plus the lower upright rectangle: $a = b + b = 2b$.

So $6b = 24$, $b = 4$, $a = 8$ and each rectangle has area $8 \cdot 4 = 32$ cm².

**Answer: (E) 32 cm²**

prompt: In the following figure, the heart and the arrow are arranged as pictured. At the same moment the heart and the arrow begin to move. The arrow moves around the figure 3 spaces clockwise and the heart 4 spaces anticlockwise and then they stop. This process repeats itself over and over again. After how many repetitions does the arrow find itself for the first time in the same triangle as the heart?

solutions.title: Relative position
solutions.body:
The figure is a heptagon divided into 7 triangles. Measure positions clockwise. In one repetition the arrow moves $+3$ and the heart $-4$, so the distance from the heart to the arrow changes by $3 - (-4) = 7$, which is a full turn. So after every repetition the two are in exactly the same relative position as at the start.

At the start they are in different triangles, so they will never be in the same triangle.

**Answer: (E) That will never happen**

solutions.title: Heart moves like the arrow
solutions.body:
Moving 4 spaces anticlockwise on 7 triangles is the same as moving $7 - 4 = 3$ spaces clockwise. So the heart and the arrow both move 3 spaces clockwise every time: they stay the same distance apart forever and never meet.

**Answer: (E) That will never happen**

prompt: In triangle $ABC$ (see sketch) $AD$ is the angle bisector of the angle at $A$ and $BH$ is the height from side $AC$. The obtuse angle between $BH$ and $AD$ is four times the size of angle $\angle DAB$. How big is the angle $\angle CAB$?

solutions.title: Triangle at H
solutions.body:
Let $\angle DAB = \angle DAC = \alpha$ and let $P$ be the point where $AD$ meets $BH$. In the right triangle $AHP$ (right angle at $H$), $\angle HAP = \alpha$, so $\angle APH = 90° - \alpha$. The obtuse angle between the two lines is $180° - (90° - \alpha) = 90° + \alpha$.

$90° + \alpha = 4\alpha$ gives $\alpha = 30°$, so $\angle CAB = 2\alpha = 60°$.

**Answer: (C) 60°**

solutions.title: Exterior angle
solutions.body:
The obtuse angle at $P$ is an exterior angle of triangle $AHP$, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $90° + \alpha$. Setting this to $4\alpha$ gives $\alpha = 30°$ and $\angle CAB = 60°$.

**Answer: (C) 60°**

prompt: Six boys live together in an apartment, which has two bathrooms. Each morning from 7:00 they use both of the bathrooms before breakfast whereby they are 8, 10, 12, 17, 21, and 22 minutes respectively, constantly alone in one of the two bathrooms. What is the earliest time that all six boys can have breakfast together?

solutions.title: Split into two groups
solutions.body:
The times add up to $8 + 10 + 12 + 17 + 21 + 22 = 90$ minutes. The boys split into two groups, one per bathroom, and breakfast can start when the busier bathroom is free. At best each bathroom is used for 45 minutes.

Is there a group summing to 45? The group containing 22 would need 23 more from $\{8, 10, 12, 17, 21\}$: no pair or triple gives 23. A group without 22 but with 21 would need 24 from $\{8, 10, 12, 17\}$: impossible. Without both, the largest possible is $8 + 10 + 12 + 17 = 47$, and dropping one number gives 39, 37, 35 or 30: not 45. So 45 is impossible.

46 works: $21 + 17 + 8 = 46$ and $22 + 12 + 10 = 44$. Earliest breakfast: 7:46.

**Answer: (B) 7:46**

prompt: The sides of a rectangle are 6 cm and 11 cm long. You select one of the long sides. Then the angle bisectors of the angles at the ends of this side are drawn. They split the opposite long side into three pieces. How long are these pieces?

solutions.title: 45° lines
solutions.body:
Each bisector of a right angle makes $45°$ with the sides, so it cuts off an isosceles right triangle. Starting at a corner of the chosen side, the bisector reaches the opposite side (6 cm away) after going 6 cm along. So the bisector from the left corner meets the opposite side 6 cm from the left, and the one from the right corner meets it 6 cm from the right, i.e. 5 cm from the left.

The pieces are 5 cm, $6 - 5 = 1$ cm and 5 cm.

**Answer: (E) 5 cm, 1 cm, 5 cm**

prompt: Captain Sparrow and his pirates loot some gold coins. They share the coins equally amongst themselves. If they were four pirates less they would each get 10 coins more. If the number of coins was 50 less, they would each get 5 coins less. How many coins did they share between themselves?

solutions.title: Use the second fact first
solutions.body:
50 coins fewer means each pirate gets 5 fewer, so there are $50 \div 5 = 10$ pirates.

With $c$ coins each, 4 fewer pirates (6) would get $c + 10$ each: $10c = 6(c + 10)$, so $4c = 60$, $c = 15$.

Total: $10 \cdot 15 = 150$.

**Answer: (D) 150**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
With 10 pirates (from the 50-coin fact): 150 coins gives 15 each, and 6 pirates would get 25 each, 10 more. ✓ For 80, 100, 120, 250 the pirates would get 8, 10, 12, 25 each, and 6 pirates would get $13.\overline{3}$, $16.\overline{6}$, 20, $41.\overline{6}$ – none is 10 more.

**Answer: (D) 150**

prompt: The average value of two positive numbers is 30% less than one of the two numbers. By which percentage is the average value bigger than the other number?

solutions.title: Algebra
solutions.body:
Let the numbers be $a$ and $b$. The average is 30% less than $a$: $\frac{a + b}{2} = 0.7a$, so $b = 0.4a$.

The average $0.7a$ compared with $b = 0.4a$: $\frac{0.7}{0.4} = 1.75$, i.e. 75% bigger.

**Answer: (A) 75%**

solutions.title: Example numbers
solutions.body:
Take $a = 10$. The average is 7, so the other number is $2 \cdot 7 - 10 = 4$. The average 7 is $3$ more than 4, and $3/4 = 75\%$.

**Answer: (A) 75%**

prompt: Andy fills a 3×3 table with all the digits from 1 to 9 so that each cell only contains one digit. He has already put the digits 1, 2, 3 and 4 in the table as shown in the diagram. Two numbers are 'neighbouring' when the cells they are in share one side. After he had finished filling in the table he noticed: The sum of the numbers neighbouring 9 equals 15. How big is the sum of the numbers neighbouring 8?

solutions.title: Where can 9 go?
solutions.body:
The corners hold 1 (top left), 3 (top right), 2 (bottom left) and 4 (bottom right). The digits 5–9 go into the four edge cells and the centre.

- 9 in the centre: its four neighbours are four of 5–8, sum at least $5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 26$. ✗
- 9 top middle: neighbours $1 + 3 +$ centre $= 15$ needs centre 11. ✗
- 9 middle left: $1 + 2 +$ centre needs 12. ✗
- 9 bottom middle: $2 + 4 +$ centre needs 9, but 9 is used. ✗
- 9 middle right: $3 + 4 +$ centre $= 15$ gives centre $= 8$. ✓

So 8 is in the centre. Its neighbours are the four edge cells: 9 and the remaining digits 5, 6, 7. Sum $= 9 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 27$.

**Answer: (E) 27**

prompt: A set of scales does not always show the correct mass. If something is less than 1000 g they show the exact mass. When something weighs 1000 g or more, they show some mass over 1000 g. You have 5 balls with the masses $A$ g, $B$ g, $C$ g, $D$ g and $E$ g each less than 1000 g. When you weigh these in pairs the scales show the following: $B + D = 1200$, $C + E = 2100$, $B + E = 800$, $B + C = 900$, $A + E = 700$. Which ball is the heaviest?

solutions.title: Use only the reliable readings
solutions.body:
Readings of 1000 g or more only tell us the true mass is at least 1000 g. So we know exactly: $B + E = 800$, $B + C = 900$, $A + E = 700$; and only $B + D \ge 1000$, $C + E \ge 1000$.

From $B + C = 900$ and $B + E = 800$: $C = E + 100$. Then $C + E = 2E + 100 \ge 1000$ gives $E \ge 450$.

Now $B = 800 - E \le 350$ and $A = 700 - E \le 250$, while $E \ge 450$ and $C = E + 100$. Finally $D \ge 1000 - B = 200 + E > E + 100 = C$.

So $D$ is heavier than $C$, which is heavier than $E$, which is heavier than $A$ and $B$.

**Answer: (D)** $D$

prompt: The quadrilateral $ABCD$ has right angles only in corners $A$ and $D$. The numbers in the diagram give the respective areas of the triangles in which they are located. How big is the area of $ABCD$?

solutions.title: Trapezium triangles
solutions.body:
Right angles at $A$ and $D$ mean $AB \parallel DC$, so $ABCD$ is a trapezium. Let $O$ be the crossing point of the diagonals.

Triangles $ABD$ and $ABC$ have the same base $AB$ and the same height, so they have equal areas. Removing the common part $AOB$ (area 5): $T = $ area $BOC$ = area $AOD = 10$.

Triangles $AOB$ and $BOC$ have the same height from $B$, so $AO : OC = 5 : 10 = 1 : 2$. Triangles $AOD$ and $DOC$ have the same height from $D$, so $S = 2 \cdot 10 = 20$.

Total: $5 + 10 + 10 + 20 = 45$.

**Answer: (B) 45**

solutions.title: Product rule
solutions.body:
For crossing diagonals in any quadrilateral, the products of opposite triangle areas are equal: $5 \cdot S = 10 \cdot T$. In a trapezium the two side triangles are equal, $T = 10$, so $S = 20$. Area $= 5 + 10 + 10 + 20 = 45$.

**Answer: (B) 45**

prompt: Jan and Eva undertake a challenge to solve mathematics questions. They each get an identical list of 100 questions. For each correctly solved question, the first to solve it gets 4 points while the slower person gets 1 point. Jan solved 60 questions and Eva also solved 60 questions. Together they score 312 points. How many questions were solved by both Jan and Eva?

solutions.title: Points per question
solutions.body:
A question solved by both gives $4 + 1 = 5$ points in total; a question solved by only one of them gives 4.

If $x$ questions were solved by both, then $60 - x$ were solved only by Jan and $60 - x$ only by Eva:

$5x + 4 \cdot 2(60 - x) = 480 - 3x = 312$, so $x = 56$.

**Answer: (D) 56**

solutions.title: Start from the maximum
solutions.body:
If no question had been solved by both, they would have $120 \cdot 4 = 480$ points. Each question solved by both replaces two 4-point solves (8 points) by $4 + 1 = 5$ points, losing 3. They lost $480 - 312 = 168 = 3 \cdot 56$ points, so 56 questions were solved by both.

**Answer: (D) 56**

prompt: David cycles from Edinburgh to his aunty who lives outside of Edinburgh. He wants to arrive at exactly 15:00 hours. After 2/3 of his planned travel time he had covered 3/4 of the way. Therefore he began to cycle slower and arrived exactly on time at his destination. In which ratio are the average speeds of the two sections of his journey?

solutions.title: Distance over time
solutions.body:
Let the total time be $T$ and the distance $d$.
- First part: $\tfrac34 d$ in $\tfrac23 T$, speed $\frac{3d/4}{2T/3} = \frac98 \cdot \frac dT$.
- Second part: $\tfrac14 d$ in $\tfrac13 T$, speed $\frac{d/4}{T/3} = \frac34 \cdot \frac dT$.

Ratio $\frac98 : \frac34 = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2$.

**Answer: (C) 3 : 2**

solutions.title: Concrete numbers
solutions.body:
Say the trip is 12 km in 3 hours. He rode 9 km in the first 2 hours (4.5 km/h) and the remaining 3 km in 1 hour (3 km/h). $4.5 : 3 = 3 : 2$.

**Answer: (C) 3 : 2**

prompt: Four identical cubes (see diagram) were fitted together. If the resulting shape is viewed from the front you see a black circle (picture on the right). What will you see on the back of the shape?

solutions.title: Opposite faces
solutions.body:
The four cubes stand in a $2 \times 2$ square. Seen from the front, each cube shows its face with the large black quarter circle, turned so that the four quarter circles meet in the middle to make a full circle. So each cube's quarter-circle corner points to the centre of the square.

From the back we see, on each cube, the face opposite the quarter-circle face. Working out from the four views of the cube which face is opposite the quarter circle, and where its marking lies, gives a short line cutting off the corner at the same edge as the centre of the quarter circle. Then all four cubes show such a corner cut at the centre of the back view, and together they form the small square (tilted by 45°) of picture (A).

**Answer: (A)**

reviewNote: Official key is (A). The solution only sketches which face of the cube lies opposite the quarter-circle face; this was not fully checked against the four perspective drawings.

prompt: A group of 25 people is made up of knights, rascals and shilly-shalliers. The knights always tell the truth, the rascals are always untruthful, and the shilly-shalliers answer alternately truthfully and falsely (or the other way around). After the first question asked to everybody, "are you a knight?" 17 of them answered "yes!" After the second question asked to everybody "are you a shilly-shallier?" 12 of them answered "yes!" After the third question asked to everybody "are you a rascal?" 8 of them answered "yes!" How many knights are in this group of people?

solutions.title: Who says yes
solutions.body:
Let there be $k$ knights and $r$ rascals. Split the shilly-shalliers into $s_1$ who answer true–false–true and $s_2$ who answer false–true–false.

| question | knight | rascal | $s_1$ (T,F,T) | $s_2$ (F,T,F) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| knight? | yes | yes | no | yes |
| shilly-shallier? | no | yes | no | yes |
| rascal? | no | no | no | yes |

So $k + r + s_2 = 17$, $r + s_2 = 12$, $s_2 = 8$. Hence $r = 4$ and $k = 17 - 12 = 5$.

(Then $s_1 = 25 - 5 - 4 - 8 = 8$, which is fine.)

**Answer: (B) 5**

prompt: Lots of different positive whole numbers were written on a blackboard. Exactly two of these numbers are divisible by 2 and exactly 13 of these numbers are divisible by 13. The biggest number on the board is $M$. What is the smallest value that $M$ can have?

solutions.title: Few even multiples of 13
solutions.body:
There are 13 different multiples of 13 on the board, $13k$ for 13 different $k$, and at most 2 of them can be even, i.e. at most 2 of the $k$ can be even. So at least 11 of the $k$ are odd. The 11 smallest odd numbers are $1, 3, \dots, 21$, so the largest $k$ is at least 21 and $M \ge 13 \cdot 21 = 273$.

$M = 273$ is possible: write $13 \cdot k$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, \dots, 21$. These are 13 numbers, exactly two of them ($26$ and $52$) are even, and the largest is 273.

**Answer: (C) 273**

prompt: On a pond 16 lilly pads are arranged in a 4×4 grid as can be seen in the diagram. A frog sits on a lilly pad in one of the corners of the grid (see picture). The frog jumps from one lilly pad to another horizontally or vertically. In doing so he always jumps over at least one lilly pad. He never lands on the same lilly pad twice. What is the maximum number of lilly pads, including the one he is sitting on, on which he can land?

solutions.title: A path through all 16
solutions.body:
Name columns a–d from left to right and rows 1–4 from bottom to top; the frog starts on a1. Every jump below goes at least two pads along a row or a column:

a1 → c1 → c3 → a3 → d3 → b3 → b1 → d1 → d4 → a4 → c4 → c2 → a2 → d2 → b2 → b4

This visits all 16 pads once each, so the maximum is 16.

**Answer: (A) 16**

prompt: A 5×5 square is covered with 1×1 tiles. The design on each tile is made up of three dark triangles and one light triangle (see diagram). The triangles of neighbouring tiles always have the same colour where they join along an edge. The border of the large square is made of dark and light triangles. What is the smallest number of dark triangles that could be amongst them?

solutions.title: Parity
solutions.body:
Each of the 25 tiles has exactly one light triangle, and each triangle lies along one edge of its tile. A light triangle on an inner edge must meet a light triangle of the neighbouring tile, so light triangles on inner edges come in pairs. Hence the number of light triangles on the border is $25 - 2p$ for some $p$: an **odd** number.

The border consists of 20 triangles, belonging to the 16 border tiles. Each tile has only one light triangle, so at most 16 border triangles are light; being odd, at most 15. So at least $20 - 15 = 5$ are dark.

5 is possible: pair up the 9 inner tiles together with one border tile next to an inner corner tile into 5 dominoes, with their light triangles facing each other inside each domino; let the other 15 border tiles show their light triangle on the border. All other edges are dark on both sides. The 4 corners and that one border tile give exactly 5 dark border triangles.

**Answer: (B) 5**
